About Roland Nielson

I got tired of living the same day

Men's life coach in Omaha. Grew up in North Omaha. Father of four boys. Coaching men since November 2025.

Book a Free Discovery Call Call or Text Roland

My story

North Omaha, chaos, and a slow turn around

I grew up in North Omaha. My mom struggled with meth. My dad wasn't around. I spent time in juvenile detention as a kid, and I carried that chaos into adulthood. Addiction, jail cells, funerals, whole nights wondering if I'd wake up. I'm not going to dress it up.

In 2011 I started changing how I lived. People always want to hear about the big moment. There wasn't one. I kept showing up. I kept my word more often than I broke it. I learned to sit with an emotion without letting it run the house. That's it. That's the secret, and it isn't much of a secret.

I'm a father of four boys. Being present with them matters more to me than looking like I have everything figured out. I don't. Some days I'm tired and short and I have to go back and apologize. But I come home, and I stay.

Dad came home. Dad stayed.

Why I coach men

Because men are quiet about this stuff until it's too late. We'll talk about trucks and football for hours and never say "I'm not okay" or "I don't know how to stop doing this." A lot of men don't have anyone who will listen without judging and then ask, "So what are you going to do about it?"

I started coaching in November 2025 to be that person for other men in Omaha. Not a guru. Not someone with a perfect life. Someone who has been in the hole, climbed out slowly, and can help you plan your own climb.

My approach is simple: Keep your word. Call your kids. Clean up your mess. Try again tomorrow.

What I believe

Healing isn't forgetting

It's remembering without bleeding. Your past doesn't disappear. It just stops running your life.

Honesty over comfort

I'll tell you what I see, respectfully. You can tell me I'm wrong. That's how real work gets done.

Your life, your plan

I don't believe one program, meeting, or method works for everybody. We look at your life and use what helps.

Small promises, kept

Self-respect comes back the same way trust does: one kept promise at a time.

No shame

Tell me what's going on. You don't need to clean it up first. I've seen worse, and I've done worse.

Hear it from me

Two short videos

One on who I work with. One on recovery and why I won't whisper about it.

A short message from Roland on coaching men in Omaha.

Plain and clear

What I'm not

I'm a non-clinical life coach. I am not a therapist, counselor, doctor or certified coach, and I don't hold a peer-recovery certification. I don't diagnose, provide therapy, manage medication or handle crisis situations.

What I bring is lived experience, honesty and a plan. If you need more than coaching, I'll tell you, and I'll help you find licensed professionals. Coaching can keep going alongside that.

In crisis? Call or text 988. Need local services? Call 211.

Accountability coaching · Omaha

Accountability that holds on a bad Tuesday

Monday you're all in. By Thursday the old habits are back. If that's your pattern, the problem isn't motivation. It's that nobody checks in.

Book a Free Discovery Call Text Roland

Last updated October 16, 2026

What do you do on a bad Tuesday?

That's the first question I ask. Not what you'll do when you feel great. What you'll do when you slept four hours, your boss chewed you out and the kids are fighting in the back seat.

Most plans are built for good days. They fall apart the first time life gets loud. Then you feel like a failure, so you quit, and three months later you start over with a new plan that also only works on good days.

Accountability coaching breaks that loop. We build a plan with a floor, the bare minimum you'll do even on the worst day, and then someone actually asks how it went. Keep your word. Clean up your mess. Try again tomorrow.

What we work on

Habits, discipline and keeping your word

We focus on the few habits that make everything else easier.

Daily structure

A morning and evening routine you can run half asleep. When the day has a shape, decisions get easier.

Consistency

Training, eating, sleep, screen time. Smaller targets you actually hit beat big ones you abandon.

Self-sabotage

Finding the moment you usually quit, and deciding ahead of time what you'll do instead.

Drinking and other habits

Cutting back or stopping, with a plan for the nights it's hardest. Not a program. Your plan.

Work and money

Following through on the job search, the side project, the budget you keep meaning to start.

Promises to people

Calling when you said you would. Showing up on time. Trust comes back one kept promise at a time.

How it works

A weekly rhythm you can count on

  1. Free call. 20 minutes. What keeps happening, what you've tried, what you want.
  2. Set the floor. In the first session we pick two or three commitments, each with a bad-day version.
  3. Report back. Every session starts with the same question: did you do what you said? No lectures. Just the truth and the next step.
  4. Adjust and raise. If something keeps failing, we change the plan. When it sticks, we add the next piece.

Sessions are in person in Omaha, by video or by phone. Hours: Tue–Fri 5:00–8:00 PM · Sat 11:00 AM–1:00 PM · Sun & Mon closed. Most men on accountability coaching pick Core Coaching at $249 a month for weekly sessions.

What changes

Keeping your word becomes normal again

No guarantees. The work is yours. But here's what tends to happen when men stop starting over:

  • You stop restarting every Monday because you never fully quit.
  • Slips get shorter. One bad day stays one bad day.
  • You trust yourself again, because you've watched yourself follow through.
  • The people around you notice you do what you say.
  • Discipline stops feeling like punishment and starts feeling like relief.

Honest fit

Who this is not for

  • Men who want to be yelled at. That's not how I work. I'm direct, not a drill sergeant.
  • Men who want me to do the work for them.
  • Anyone who needs medical detox, medication management, therapy or crisis care. Coaching can work alongside that support but does not replace it.

If you're not sure, call (402) 577-0738 and ask. I'll tell you straight.

Questions

Accountability coaching questions

What does an accountability coach do?

An accountability coach helps you set specific commitments and then checks that you did them. We agree on a few clear actions each week. Next session you report back: done, not done, and what got in the way. No shaming. We adjust the plan until it fits your real life, then we raise the bar a little.

How is this different from an accountability partner or a buddy?

A buddy is great, but buddies let things slide because they like you and don't want it to get awkward. I like you too, and I'll still ask the question. I also bring structure: a written plan, a weekly rhythm and a way to adjust when something keeps failing. That's harder to get from a friend.

What if I miss a week or fall off completely?

Then we talk about it, and we start again. Falling off is part of the process, not the end of it. Most of the useful work happens right after a slip, when we figure out what actually broke. The goal is not a perfect streak. The goal is getting back up faster each time.

Can you help with discipline at the gym, with money or with drinking?

Yes, coaching can help with the habits around all three: showing up to train, tracking spending, cutting back or quitting drinking. I am not a trainer, financial advisor or medical provider, so I won't write a workout or a budget. I help you decide what you'll do and then hold you to it.

How many goals should I work on at once?

Usually two or three, not ten. Men who try to fix everything at once burn out by week two. We pick the changes that make the rest easier, like sleep, a morning routine or one hard conversation. When those stick, we add more. Slow is faster than starting over every month.

Feeling Stuck at 40? 7 Signs It's Time to Rebuild (and Where to Start)

By Roland Nielson · Published October 16, 2026 · Last updated October 16, 2026 · 4 min read

Somewhere around 40, a lot of men hit a quiet wall.

Nothing is on fire. You have a job, maybe a family, maybe a house. But you wake up and feel like you’re living the same day on repeat. The things you said you’d do “someday” are still on the list. And a voice you’ve been ignoring is getting louder: is this it?

People call that a midlife crisis. I don’t love the term. Most men I talk to aren’t buying sports cars. They’re tired, stuck and not sure where to start. That’s not a crisis. It’s a signal.

Here are seven signs it’s time to rebuild, and what to do about it.

1. You’re busy all the time but nothing is moving

Your calendar is full. You’re exhausted every night. But if someone asked what you’ve built in the last two years, you’d struggle to answer. Busy is not the same as moving. When everything is urgent, the important stuff, like your health, your marriage and your goals, gets pushed to “later” forever.

2. You’ve stopped making plans for yourself

At 25 you had ideas. At 40 your plans are mostly other people’s: work deadlines, kids’ schedules, family obligations. Those matter. But a man with no plans of his own slowly starts to resent everyone else’s.

3. You’re numbing more than you used to

An extra drink most nights. Hours on the phone. Food, porn, gambling, games, whatever takes the edge off. Nobody would call it a problem. But if you need something every night to stop feeling the day, the day is telling you something.

4. Your fuse is shorter at home

You snap at your kids over small stuff. You and your partner talk about schedules and bills and not much else. You feel guilty after, but it keeps happening. Short fuses usually aren’t about the dishes. They’re about pressure with nowhere to go.

5. You keep starting over

New diet in January. New gym plan in April. New budget in September. Each one lasts a few weeks. You’re not lazy. You’re running plans that only work on good days, with nobody checking in when the bad days come.

6. You can’t remember the last time you felt proud of yourself

Not proud of your kids or your team. Proud of you. For keeping a promise, finishing something hard, or handling a tough moment well. When that feeling goes missing for years, confidence goes with it.

7. You’re second-guessing every decision

Should you take the job? Have the conversation? Move? Quit? You go back and forth for months and end up doing nothing, which is still a decision. Self-doubt grows when you haven’t watched yourself follow through in a while.

If three or more of those hit, here’s where to start

You don’t need to blow up your life. You need to rebuild it a piece at a time. Start with these three.

Start with your mornings and evenings

Before you fix your career or your marriage, fix the edges of your day. What time you go to bed. What you do the first 30 minutes after you wake up. What you do the first 30 minutes after you get home. Those three windows shape everything else. Make tomorrow easier by setting it up tonight.

Make one promise and keep it for 30 days

Pick something small and specific. Walk 20 minutes a day. No phone at dinner. In bed by 11. Then keep it, every day, for a month. When you miss, and you might, start again the next day without drama.

Keeping one small promise rebuilds something you lost: the ability to trust yourself. Do what you said. That’s where confidence actually comes from.

Say it out loud to someone

Stuck men are usually quiet men. Tell someone what you’re really thinking: your wife, a friend, a brother, a pastor, a coach. Not to get advice. Just to stop carrying it alone. Things that feel huge in your head often look a lot more solvable once they’re said out loud.

Stuck at 40 isn’t the end of the story

I was nowhere close to having it together at 30. I grew up in North Omaha with a lot of chaos, and I carried it into adulthood. I started changing in 2011, not with one big moment, but by showing up, keeping my word a little more often and learning to sit with a hard feeling without letting it run the house.

Now I’m a dad of four boys, and I coach men who are where I was: tired of living the same day.

If that’s you, read more about life coaching for men in Omaha. If you’re ready for a full reset across work, habits and home, look at the Rebuild Program. Or just book a free 20-minute call and tell me what keeps happening.

Feeling stuck is common. Feeling hopeless or unsafe is different. If you’re having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 now.

How Much Does a Life Coach Cost in Omaha? (2026 Prices Explained)

By Roland Nielson · Published October 16, 2026 · Last updated October 16, 2026 · 3 min read

If you’ve searched “how much does a life coach cost,” you’ve probably noticed something: most coaches don’t tell you. You get a “book a call to learn more” button and a sales conversation.

I think that’s backwards. Here’s a straight breakdown of what coaching costs, what drives the price, and what I charge.

The short answer

Across the US, one-on-one life coaching commonly ranges from about $75 to $300+ per session. Monthly packages often land somewhere between $200 and $1,000 a month. Coaches who work with executives or sell big-name programs can charge far more, sometimes thousands for a package.

Omaha prices tend to sit inside that national range. You’ll find some coaches lower and some much higher, depending on who they work with and what’s included.

My coaching costs $149 to $399 a month. Details below.

Per session vs monthly plans

There are two common ways coaches charge:

Per session. You pay for each meeting. It’s flexible, but it makes it easy to skip weeks, and skipping weeks is exactly what kills progress.

Monthly plans or packages. You pay a set amount for a set number of sessions per month, often with a minimum commitment. This builds a rhythm. Change comes from consistency, so I think monthly plans fit most men better.

What drives the price of a life coach

  • Session length and frequency. Weekly 60-minute sessions cost more than twice-monthly 45-minute ones.
  • Contact between sessions. Texts, check-ins and extra support add value and cost.
  • Who the coach works with. Executive coaching is usually priced for company budgets.
  • In person vs online. In-person sessions can carry room costs. Video and phone usually don’t.
  • Program length. Longer, structured programs often cost more overall but include more support.
  • Credentials and branding. Some coaches price based on certifications, books or audience size. That doesn’t always mean better coaching for you.

What I charge, and why

PlanWhat you getPrice
Starter2 × 45-minute sessions a month$149/month
Core Coaching4 × 45-minute sessions a month$249/month
Focused Support4 × 60-minute sessions a month$399/month
Founding Client (first 3 only)Core Coaching, 3-month commitment$199/month ($597 total)
In-person add-onPer in-person session, covers the room+$40

There’s also the Rebuild Program, a 3–6 month high-accountability program with weekly sessions plus check-ins in between. Pricing for that is shared on the free call.

I priced these so working men in Omaha can afford weekly support. That works out to roughly $62 to $100 per session. Video and phone sessions never cost extra. Full details are on the pricing page.

Is a life coach worth the money?

Honest answer: only if you use it.

Coaching isn’t magic. You’ll still do the work. What you’re paying for is structure, an outside view and someone who asks every week whether you did what you said you’d do. For a lot of men, that weekly check-in is the missing piece.

A useful way to decide: look at what the old pattern already costs you. Lost work. Money spent numbing out. Arguments at home. Weekends spent recovering instead of living. If coaching helps you change even one of those, it often pays for itself.

If you won’t show up or be honest, it won’t be worth it. I’ll tell you that on the first call.

Does insurance cover life coaching?

No. Life coaching isn’t a medical service, so health insurance doesn’t cover it, and it usually isn’t eligible for HSA or FSA funds. Some employers pay for coaching through professional development budgets, so it’s worth asking.

If you need care for a mental health condition or addiction, that's a different service and may be covered by insurance. Read life coach vs therapist for help telling them apart.

Questions to ask any coach before you pay

  1. What exactly is included each month?
  2. Is there a minimum commitment? What are the cancellation terms?
  3. Who do you usually work with?
  4. What happens if I miss a session?
  5. What don’t you do? (A good coach will be clear about this.)
  6. Can I talk to you for free first?

Start with the free call

Every plan I offer starts with a free 20-minute discovery call. You’ll know the price before we talk, and you’ll know whether we’re a fit before you pay a dollar.

How to Be More Present With Your Kids When Work and Life Pull You Away

By Roland Nielson · Published October 16, 2026 · Last updated October 16, 2026 · 4 min read

I didn’t have a dad around growing up. I know what that absence feels like from the kid’s side.

Now I’m a father of four boys, and here’s what I’ve learned: you can be home every night and still be absent. Your body is at the table. Your head is still at work, in your inbox, in the bills, in your phone.

Kids notice. They always notice.

The good news is that being present isn’t about big trips or expensive gifts. It’s about small, repeated moments where your kid gets all of you. Here’s how to build more of them, even when work and life keep pulling you away.

Start before you walk in the door

Most dads lose the evening in the first five minutes. You walk in still carrying the day: the argument with a coworker, the traffic, the money stress. The first thing your kid says gets the leftover tension.

Try a reset before you go inside:

  • Sit in the truck for three minutes with the radio off.
  • Take a few slow breaths.
  • Ask yourself: what kind of dad do I want to be for the next two hours?
  • Then walk in.

It sounds too simple to matter. It’s one of the most useful habits I know. Stop before you react, starting at the front door.

Give the first 15 minutes away

Make the first 15 minutes after you get home theirs. Not your phone’s, not the TV’s, not the mail’s. Get down on their level. Ask a real question. Listen to the whole answer, even if it’s a long story about a video game.

Fifteen minutes of full attention beats three hours of half attention. Kids don’t measure time the way we do. They measure whether you were really there.

Make phone rules you’ll actually keep

Your phone is the biggest thief of presence. “I’m just checking one thing” turns into twenty minutes, and your kid learns that the screen matters more.

Rules that tend to stick:

  • Phone in a drawer or another room during dinner. Everyone’s, including yours.
  • No phone for the first 30 minutes home.
  • No phone at bedtime. Bedtime talks are often when kids say the real stuff.

If work needs you reachable, set a specific check time instead of carrying it around all night.

Build small rituals

Kids remember rituals more than events. A ritual is just something you do together, regularly, that’s yours:

  • Saturday breakfast at the same diner.
  • A drive to school where you each say one good thing about the day ahead.
  • A ten-minute walk after dinner.
  • A bedtime question: “What was the best part of today? What was the hardest?”
  • Shooting hoops in the driveway before homework.

Pick one. Keep it going for a month. Small and regular beats big and rare.

One-on-one time matters

If you have more than one kid, each one needs some time where they don’t have to share you. It doesn’t have to be long. A trip to the hardware store with one kid. Twenty minutes of catch. Letting one of them help you fix something.

With four boys, I’ve learned that each of them opens up differently. Some talk while doing something with their hands. Some talk in the car, when they don’t have to look at you. Find the setting where your kid talks.

When you snap, clean it up

You’re going to lose your temper sometimes. Every dad does. What matters most is what happens next.

Go back. Get on their level. Say it simply: “I yelled at you earlier. That wasn’t okay. I’m sorry. I was stressed and I took it out on you.”

No “but.” No long speech. Then move on.

When you repair, your kid learns two things: that they matter, and how a man takes responsibility. That lesson lasts longer than the yelling. Clean up your mess. Try again tomorrow.

Be present with your partner too

Your kids are watching how you treat their mom or your partner. Being present at home includes her. Ask how her day really was. Put the phone down when she talks. Handle bedtime so she gets a break. Kids feel safer in a house where the adults are a team.

Make it a plan, not a mood

Being present can’t depend on how you feel, because some days you’ll feel wiped out. Write it down like any other commitment:

  1. My reset before I walk in.
  2. My phone rules.
  3. One ritual I’ll start this week.
  4. One-on-one time with each kid this month.
  5. How I’ll repair when I mess up.

Then check yourself at the end of each week. Did you do what you said?

Dad came home. Dad stayed.

That’s the line I live by. Not perfect. Present.

If you want help building this into your real week, with someone checking in, read about coaching for fathers and husbands in Omaha. If following through is the hard part, accountability coaching might be the better fit. Or book a free 20-minute call and tell me what keeps getting in the way.

If anger at home has turned into violence or fear, please get professional help now. In crisis, call or text 988. In danger, call 911.

Life Coach vs Therapist: Which One Do You Need? (Honest Answer)

By Roland Nielson · Published October 16, 2026 · Last updated October 16, 2026 · 3 min read

I’m a life coach. So you might expect me to tell you a coach is all you need. I won’t, because it isn’t always true, and getting this wrong can cost a man a lot.

Here’s the honest answer.

The short version

A therapist is a licensed mental health professional. They can assess and treat conditions like depression, anxiety, PTSD and addiction. They’re trained to work with trauma and with what’s happening underneath your patterns.

A life coach like me is not a licensed professional. Coaching doesn’t diagnose or treat anything. It helps a man who is stable enough to function set goals, build habits, follow through and stay accountable. It’s focused on what you do next, not on healing what happened before.

Both can help. They do different jobs.

When you need a therapist (or a doctor) first

See a licensed professional, not a coach, if any of these are true:

  • You’re having thoughts of harming yourself or someone else. Call or text 988 right now.
  • You can’t get out of bed, go to work or take care of basic things for weeks at a time.
  • Trauma, flashbacks or panic are running your life.
  • You’re drinking or using and can’t stop, or stopping makes you physically sick. That can be dangerous to do alone.
  • There’s violence or fear in your home.
  • You think you might have a condition that needs medication or a diagnosis.

A coach is the wrong tool for these, and a good coach will tell you so. When it fits, I refer men to licensed professionals.

When a life coach is a good fit

Coaching tends to work well when:

  • You’re functioning, but stuck. Same day on repeat.
  • You know what you should do and don’t do it consistently.
  • You want structure: routines, habits, a plan for the bad days.
  • You want someone to hold you to what you said.
  • You’re rebuilding after a hard chapter and want help with the practical side: work, money, relationships, routine.
  • You’d rather talk to a regular guy who’s been through it than sit in an office.

When you might want both

Plenty of men do both, and it can work well. A therapist helps you understand and heal what’s underneath. A coach helps you turn that into daily action and keeps you accountable between appointments.

If you already see a therapist, tell them you’re working with a coach, and tell your coach what you’re comfortable sharing. Coaching should support that work, never compete with it.

Cost: life coach vs therapist

Therapy is often covered at least partly by health insurance, depending on your plan. Coaching is not covered by insurance because it isn’t a medical service.

Coaching prices vary a lot nationally, from under $100 a session to several hundred. My plans run $149 to $399 a month. You can see exactly what’s included on my pricing page. If cost is your main concern and you need clinical care, check what your insurance covers first, or call 211 for low-cost local options.

What about men who “don’t do therapy”?

A lot of men tell me they’d never see a therapist. Sometimes that’s pride. Sometimes they had a bad experience. Sometimes they just don’t want to sit on a couch and talk about their childhood.

I get it. But I’d push back a little: if you need clinical help, the right professional is worth trying, and there are therapists who are direct, practical and good with men. Don’t let a stereotype keep you from help that could change your life.

If you don’t need clinical help and just need structure, honesty and someone in your corner, that’s what coaching is for.

About me, so you know who’s talking

I’m Roland Nielson, a men’s life coach in Omaha. I’m not certified, licensed or clinically trained. What I bring is lived experience: I grew up in North Omaha around addiction, spent time in juvenile detention, and started rebuilding my life in 2011. I’m a father of four boys. I’ve been coaching men since November 2025.

I don’t diagnose, provide therapy, manage medication or handle crises. I help men build a plan and keep it.

Still not sure?

That’s what the free call is for. In 20 minutes I’ll ask a few honest questions and tell you straight whether coaching makes sense, or whether you’d be better served starting somewhere else. Either way, you’ll leave with a next step.

Rebuilding Trust After Addiction: What Actually Helps (From Someone Who's Been There)

By Roland Nielson · Published October 16, 2026 · Last updated October 16, 2026 · 4 min read

When you get clean, you want everyone to see it right away. You’ve changed. You’re working hard. Why are they still checking your eyes when you walk in? Why does your wife still look at the bank account? Why does your mom still hesitate when you ask to borrow the car?

I’ve been there. I lived addiction. I lived chaos. I’ve been the guy nobody believed, and honestly, for a long time, they were right not to.

Here’s what I’ve learned about rebuilding trust. It’s slower than you want, but it works.

Understand why they don’t trust you yet

Your family didn’t stop trusting you over one thing. They stopped after dozens of broken promises, lies, missed events and scary nights. Every time you said “this time is different,” they believed you, and it wasn’t.

So your words don’t count much right now. That’s not cruelty. It’s self-protection. They’re waiting to see if you’re for real.

You can’t argue someone into trusting you. You have to show them, over time.

Stop making big promises

Big promises are what got you here. “I’ll never drink again.” “I’m going to make it all up to you.” “Everything’s going to be different.”

You might mean it. They’ve heard it before.

Make small promises instead, and keep every one:

  • “I’ll be home by 6.” Then be home at 5:55.
  • “I’ll call you after my meeting.” Then call.
  • “I’ll pick the kids up Saturday.” Then be early.

Small kept promises add up. Do what you said. That’s how trust comes back, one kept promise at a time.

Be honest about the small stuff

Addiction trains you to lie about everything, even things that don’t matter. Where you were. What you spent. Why you were late. Breaking that habit takes practice.

Tell the truth about small things, especially the inconvenient ones. “I’m running late because I stopped to talk to a buddy.” “I spent $40 on lunch this week, more than I planned.”

When your family sees you being honest about small things, they slowly start to believe you on big ones.

Own the damage without making it about you

At some point you’ll need to talk about what happened. Do it without excuses and without asking for anything back.

“I know I put you through a lot. I lied to you. I missed things that mattered. I’m sorry, and I’m working on it every day.”

Then stop. Don’t follow it with “so can you start trusting me?” Don’t make them comfort you. Let them have their feelings, even if they’re angry. That anger is part of the healing too.

Healing isn’t forgetting. It’s remembering without bleeding. You don’t have to pretend the past didn’t happen. You just have to stop letting it run your life.

Let them have their guard up

Your wife may want to see your phone. Your parents may want to know where you’re going. It can feel insulting when you’re doing everything right.

Try to see it as part of the price of rebuilding, not a punishment. Being open on purpose, before anyone asks, speeds things up: share your schedule, tell them about meetings, offer the information.

That said, healthy boundaries matter on both sides. Rebuilding trust doesn’t mean being treated like a prisoner forever. If things get stuck, a professional who works with families can help you all sort it out.

Build a life that makes relapse harder

Trust rebuilds faster when your life has structure. Empty hours and old routines are where trouble finds you.

  • Fill your days on purpose: work, meetings, exercise, family time.
  • Know your hardest hours of the week and have a plan for them.
  • Keep people around you who want you to win.
  • Have someone to call when a bad day is building.

A plan matters most when you’re angry, tired, broke, lonely, or ready to quit. Write it down before you need it.

Give it time. More than you want to.

There’s no set timeline. For some families it’s months. For others, years. Some relationships come back stronger than before. Some take longer than you’d like. You don’t control that part.

What you control: showing up, keeping your word, being honest and cleaning up your mess when you slip. Keep doing that, and most people eventually notice.

You don’t have to do it alone

When I started changing in 2011, there was no big moment. I kept showing up. I kept my word more often. I learned to sit with an emotion without letting it run the house. Now I’m a father of four boys, and the people I hurt can count on me.

If you’re rebuilding and want structure and accountability alongside your recovery support, read about coaching for men rebuilding after addiction. If you’re a family member, this page is for you. Or book a free 20-minute call and tell me where you are.

Coaching is not addiction care and does not replace meetings, a sponsor or professional support. If you’re in crisis, call or text 988. For local resources, call 211.

What to Do on a Bad Tuesday: A Simple Plan for When Motivation Disappears

By Roland Nielson · Published October 16, 2026 · Last updated October 16, 2026 · 4 min read

Everybody has a plan for Monday. Monday you’re rested, the week is clean, and you’re going to eat right, hit the gym, call your mom and stop scrolling at midnight.

Then Tuesday shows up.

You slept four hours. The truck needs a part you can’t afford. Your boss found the one mistake you made. Your kid has a meltdown in the car and you yell louder than you meant to. By 8 PM you’re on the couch with a drink and your phone, and the plan from Monday feels like it was written by somebody else.

That’s the day I care about. The first question I ask every man I coach is: what do you do on a bad Tuesday?

Why most plans fail on bad days

Most plans are written by your best self, for your best self. They assume you’ll have energy, time and a good mood. Those are the three things you never have on a bad day.

So the plan breaks. And because it broke, you feel like you failed. And because you feel like you failed, you quit the whole thing. Three weeks later you start over with a new plan that also only works on good days.

That loop isn’t a character problem. It’s a design problem. A plan matters most when you’re angry, tired, broke, lonely, or ready to quit. If it doesn’t work then, it doesn’t work.

Step 1: Set a floor, not just a goal

A goal is what you’ll do on a good day. A floor is the least you’ll do on the worst day.

  • Goal: work out for an hour. Floor: 10 push-ups before bed.
  • Goal: no drinking this week. Floor: no drinking before 8 PM, and text someone if you want to.
  • Goal: read to the kids every night. Floor: two minutes of real attention at bedtime, phone in another room.
  • Goal: get the budget done. Floor: open the bank app and look.

The floor should feel almost too easy. That’s the point. On a bad Tuesday you don’t need a big win. You need to not break the chain. Keeping a tiny promise to yourself on a terrible day does more for your confidence than a great workout on a good one.

Step 2: Know your warning signs

Bad days rarely come out of nowhere. They build. Most men have the same three or four early signs every time:

  • Skipping lunch, then getting home starving and short-tempered.
  • Staying up too late two nights in a row.
  • Going quiet with your partner instead of saying you’re stressed.
  • Checking out with your phone the minute you get home.

Write yours down. When you notice two of them stacking up, that’s your cue to switch to the bad-day plan before the day goes sideways, not after.

Step 3: Have a 10-minute reset

When the day is already bad, you need something you can do in 10 minutes that changes the direction of the evening. Mine is simple: step outside, walk around the block, drink some water, and decide one thing I’m going to do before bed.

Yours might be a shower, a drive with the radio off, a few minutes in the garage, or sitting in the truck for five minutes before you walk in the door. The rule: you do it before you react. Stop before you react. That pause is where most of the damage gets prevented.

Step 4: Decide who you’ll text

Isolation turns a bad day into a bad week. Pick one or two people you’ll text when it’s going wrong. Not to fix it. Just to say it out loud.

“Rough day. Not going to drink tonight. Checking in.”

That’s it. Saying it to someone makes it real, and it’s harder to break a promise someone else heard. If you have a sponsor, a friend from church, a brother or a coach, put their name in your plan now, while you’re calm.

Step 5: Make tomorrow easier

On a bad Tuesday, the best thing you can do is set up Wednesday. Make tomorrow easier.

  • Put the dishes in the sink, at least.
  • Lay out clothes for the morning.
  • Set the alarm and put the phone across the room.
  • Write down the one thing that matters most tomorrow.

None of these take more than a few minutes. All of them mean Wednesday-you starts ahead instead of behind.

Step 6: Clean up your mess

If you blew it, and sometimes you will, own it fast. Apologize to your wife or your kid without a speech and without “but.” “I was short with you earlier. That wasn’t fair. I’m sorry.”

Then let it go and try again tomorrow. Keep your word. Call your kids. Clean up your mess. Try again tomorrow. That’s not a slogan. It’s the whole plan.

Write your bad-Tuesday plan tonight

Grab a notecard and write:

  1. My floor for each habit.
  2. My three warning signs.
  3. My 10-minute reset.
  4. The person I’ll text.
  5. One thing I’ll do to make tomorrow easier.

Put it somewhere you’ll see it. On a bad day you won’t remember the plan. You’ll only follow what’s in front of you.

When a plan isn’t enough

A notecard helps. But the reason most men slip is that nobody checks in. That’s what accountability coaching in Omaha is built for: we write your plan together, including the bad-day version, and then every week I ask how it went.

If you’ve been restarting every Monday for years, book a free 20-minute call. Tell me what keeps happening. You don’t need to clean it up first.

If a bad day ever turns into thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 right away.

Be the dad who comes home and stays

Maybe you come home wrung out and snap at small things. Maybe you're on your phone through dinner. Maybe you and your wife only talk about schedules and bills. None of that makes you a bad man. It makes you a tired one without a plan.

I'm a father of four boys. Being present with them matters more to me than looking like I have everything figured out. That's what I help other dads work toward.

Dad came home. Dad stayed.

What we work on

Being a better father and husband, one week at a time

Coming home well

A short reset between work and home so your family gets you, not what's left of you.

Patience under pressure

Stop before you react. Catch the build-up and choose your words before they choose themselves.

Time with your kids

Small, regular rituals that matter more to kids than big trips: rides, games, bedtime talks.

Talking with your partner

Fewer schedule meetings, more real conversations. Listening without fixing. Repairing after a fight.

Breaking old patterns

Noticing what you inherited from your own father, and deciding what stops with you.

Rebuilding after divorce

Being a steady dad on your days and building a life you respect on your own.

How sessions work

Built around work and family

Dads don't have spare afternoons. That's why I coach evenings and Saturdays: Tue–Fri 5:00–8:00 PM · Sat 11:00 AM–1:00 PM · Sun & Mon closed.

  • Phone on the drive home, before you walk in the door.
  • Video after the kids are asleep.
  • In person in Omaha by appointment, at your location or a private meeting space. A walk around Standing Bear Lake works too.

Every session ends with a couple of specific things to try at home this week. Next time, we talk about how it went. See coaching plans and prices.

What changes

What families notice first

I can't promise outcomes. Your family's story is yours. These are the changes dads describe most:

  • Fewer blowups, and faster apologies when they happen.
  • Kids who come to you with stuff, because you've been listening.
  • A partner who feels like a teammate again.
  • Evenings with a little calm in them.
  • You like the dad you're becoming.

Honest fit

Who this is not for

  • Families dealing with abuse or violence at home. That needs professional help and safety planning first. Call 911 in an emergency, or 988 for crisis support.
  • Couples looking for marriage counseling. I coach the man, one-on-one.
  • Dads who want a script to make their kids behave. This is about you, not them.

Questions

Questions dads ask

How can I be more present with my family?

Start small and specific. Put the phone in another room for the first 30 minutes after you get home. Ask each kid one real question at dinner. Plan one thing a week that is just you and them. In coaching we build habits like these into your actual schedule and check that they happen.

Can coaching help with my temper at home?

Yes, coaching can help you stop before you react. We look at what sets you off, when it happens and what your body does right before. Then we build a pause and a plan for those moments. If anger is leading to violence or fear in the home, you need more than coaching, and I will help you find it.

I work long hours. Can coaching fit around that?

Yes. I coach evenings and Saturdays for exactly that reason. Hours are Tue–Fri 5:00–8:00 PM · Sat 11:00 AM–1:00 PM · Sun & Mon closed. Sessions can happen by phone on the drive home or by video after the kids are in bed. No need to take time off work.

Do you work with divorced or separated dads?

Yes. Rebuilding after divorce is one of the hardest seasons a man goes through. We work on being a steady dad on your days, keeping communication with your ex civil, and building a life you respect on your own. I do not give legal advice, but I can help you stay level while you deal with it.

Can my wife be part of the sessions?

Coaching is one-on-one with you. Your wife or partner is welcome to book the free call or ask questions, and some men choose to share their plan at home. What you say in session stays private unless you decide to share it. Couples work is a different service, and I can point you to it.

Questions men ask

Straight answers

What coaching is, what it costs in Omaha, how sessions work, and what I don't do. If your question isn't here, call or text and ask.

What does a life coach do?

A life coach helps you get clear on what you want, build a simple plan and stick to it. With me that means weekly sessions, honest questions and accountability. We look at where your days go, what keeps knocking you off track and what to do on a bad day. You do the work. I help you keep showing up for it.

How much does a life coach cost in Omaha?

My coaching costs $149 to $399 a month. Starter is $149 for two 45-minute sessions, Core Coaching is $249 for four, and Focused Support is $399 for four 60-minute sessions. The first three Founding Clients get Core Coaching for $199 a month for three months. In-person sessions add $40 to cover the room. The first call is free. See full pricing.

Do I need a life coach or a therapist?

You need a therapist if you are dealing with a mental health condition, trauma that is taking over, or thoughts of harming yourself. A coach helps a stable man build structure, habits and follow-through. I am a non-clinical coach, not a therapist. Many men do both. If I think you need more than coaching, I will tell you and point you to licensed help.

Is life coaching legit if the coach is not certified?

Yes, coaching is not a licensed field, and certification is optional. I am not certified. I bring lived experience: I grew up in North Omaha, rebuilt my life starting in 2011 and raise four boys. Judge me on the free call, not a certificate. If it does not feel useful after 20 minutes, you walk away and owe nothing.

What happens on the free discovery call?

The free call is 20 minutes on the phone. You tell me what keeps happening, what you have tried and what you want different. I ask a few straight questions and tell you honestly whether I can help. If it is a fit, we pick a plan and a start date. If not, I will point you somewhere better. No pressure either way.

What happens in the first coaching session?

In the first session we map your week and pick what matters most. We look at sleep, work, family, money, anger, habits, whatever is pulling you under. Then we set two or three small commitments you can keep before the next session. You leave with a plan you can follow on a bad day, not a list of 40 goals.

Where do in-person sessions happen in Omaha?

In-person sessions happen at your location or a private meeting space in Omaha, by appointment. Some men like a walk-and-talk on the Keystone Trail or around Zorinsky Lake. In-person sessions add $40 each to cover room costs. Video and phone sessions have no extra fee. See the areas I serve.

Do you offer evening and Saturday sessions?

Yes. I coach Tuesday to Friday from 5:00 to 8:00 PM and Saturday from 11:00 AM to 1:00 PM, Central time. Sunday and Monday are closed. Evenings and Saturdays exist on purpose: most men I work with have jobs and kids, and they cannot leave work at 2 PM to talk about their life.

Can we meet by video or phone instead?

Yes. Video and phone sessions work the same as in person and cost nothing extra. Plenty of men take calls from the truck, the garage or a walk around the block. Video works anywhere in Nebraska and beyond, so moving or traveling for work does not have to break the routine.

Is coaching confidential?

Yes. What you tell me stays between us. I do not share it with your wife, parents, boss or anyone else without your permission. The exceptions are if someone is at risk of serious harm or the law requires it. Coaching does not carry legal privilege the way some professions do, and I will explain that plainly on the first call.

How long does it take to see results?

Most men notice something small within the first few weeks: a calmer evening, a kept promise, a better morning. Bigger change takes months of showing up. I do not promise results, because the work is yours. I promise to be honest, to be prepared and to hold you to what you said you would do.

Is there a commitment or cancellation policy?

The Founding Client rate is a 3-month commitment. For the other plans, we go over cancellation and rescheduling terms on the free call, before you pay anything or pick a plan. Ask whatever you want about it. You should know exactly what you are agreeing to before we start working together.

Can my wife or parent book a call for me?

Yes, a wife, partner or parent can book the free call or reach out for you. But coaching only works if you choose it. On the call I will talk with you directly, and you decide. Families can pay for coaching, and I still keep what you share private. More for families.

Do you work with men in recovery?

Yes. Some of the men I work with are rebuilding after addiction or a hard stretch. I bring lived experience, not a program. Coaching helps with structure, routine, accountability and rebuilding trust. It is not a replacement for meetings, sponsors or professional care. It works alongside them. Coaching for men rebuilding after addiction.

What don't you do?

I do not diagnose, provide therapy or psychotherapy, give medical advice, manage medication or handle crisis situations. I am a non-clinical life coach. If you need any of that, I will help you find licensed professionals. If you are in crisis right now, call or text 988. For local services and resources, call 211.

What areas do you serve?

I coach men across the Omaha metro: Omaha, Bellevue, Papillion, La Vista, Ralston, Millard, Elkhorn, Gretna, Bennington, Council Bluffs (IA). In-person sessions happen by appointment anywhere in that area. Video and phone sessions work from anywhere, including the rest of Nebraska and western Iowa.

Who is coaching with Roland for?

It is for men, mostly 30 to 55, who are tired of living the same day. Fathers who want to be present. Working men who are stretched thin. Men rebuilding after addiction, divorce or a setback. Men who start strong and slip. If you are willing to be honest and do the work, we will get along fine.

Is a life coach worth it?

A life coach is worth it if you will use the help. Coaching costs less than many habits that are costing you now: lost work, lost sleep, arguments at home. The value is in showing up every week and keeping small promises. Start with the free call and decide after you have talked to me, not before.

I've tried programs and meetings before. Why would this be different?

Maybe it will not be, and I will not pretend otherwise. I do not believe one program, meeting or method works for everybody. We look at your actual life and use what helps. Men often slip because nobody checks in on a bad Tuesday. That check-in is a big part of what I do.

For wives, partners and parents

When someone you love keeps getting stuck

You can see what he could be. He keeps falling back into the same patterns. Here's how coaching might help, what it can't do, and how to bring it up.

Book a Free Call for Him Text Roland

Last updated October 16, 2026

Need immediate crisis help? Call or text 988. Need local services or resources? Call 211. Coaching is not crisis support. If you are in danger, call 911.

You're not the only one carrying this

Maybe it's your husband. He works hard, but he comes home angry or checked out. Maybe he drinks more than he used to. Maybe he keeps saying he'll change, and you've stopped believing it.

Maybe it's your son. He's grown, but stuck. Bouncing between jobs, couches or bad decisions. You've helped, and helped, and you're not sure if you're helping anymore.

A lot of the calls I get start with someone who loves a man and is worried about him. That's not overstepping. It's caring. You can make the call. He has to make the choice.

How to bring it up

Talk to him like a teammate, not a project

  1. Pick a calm moment. Not during a fight, not when he's been drinking, not in front of the kids.
  2. Lead with what you love. "I see how hard you work. I miss you being here with us."
  3. Be specific. Name what you've seen: the late nights, the temper, the missed promises. Skip the labels.
  4. Offer one small step. "There's a coach in Omaha who does free 20-minute calls. Evenings work. Would you try one?"
  5. Let him decide. Pressure usually backfires. Leave the link and let it sit.

Some men respond better to a man who has been there. You can share Roland's story or the rebuilding after addiction page and let it speak for itself.

What coaching can do

  • Give him a plan for his week, including the bad days.
  • Hold him accountable every week, so it's not your job.
  • Help him handle stress and anger before it lands on the family.
  • Support him in being present with you and the kids.
  • Help rebuild trust through kept promises over time.

What coaching can't do

  • Diagnose or treat addiction, depression or any condition.
  • Replace therapy, medical care, detox or treatment programs.
  • Handle a crisis. Call or text 988, or 911 in danger.
  • Make him change if he doesn't want to.
  • Fix a marriage on its own. I coach him one-on-one.

Confidentiality

What stays private

What he tells me stays between him and me, even if you book the call or pay for the plan. That privacy is why men open up. I'll tell you this before we start, so there are no surprises.

He can share as much as he wants with you. Many men end up showing their plan to their wife or parents. If someone is at risk of serious harm, safety comes first.

Booking for him

How to book a call on his behalf

  1. Book the free 20-minute call, call or text (402) 577-0738, or use the contact form and pick "Someone I care about."
  2. We talk first: what's going on, what you've tried, what you hope for.
  3. Then I talk with him directly. He decides whether to go ahead.
  4. If he does, you can pay for his plan. See coaching prices.

Looking after yourself matters too. My page of Omaha resources includes family groups and helplines.

Questions

Questions families ask

Can I book a coaching call for my husband or son?

Yes. You can book the free 20-minute call, call or text, or fill out the contact form and choose "Someone I care about." I'll talk with you about what's going on. Then I need to talk with him directly, because coaching only works if he chooses to take part.

Will you tell me what he says in sessions?

No. What he shares stays between him and me, even if you're paying. That privacy is a big reason men open up. He is free to share his plan or progress with you, and many men do. The exception is if someone is at risk of serious harm.

Can I pay for coaching for my adult son?

Yes. Parents often pay for coaching for an adult son at a crossroads. You can pay for the plan, and I'll still treat him as the client. We can agree up front on what, if anything, he's comfortable having me confirm with you, such as whether he's attending sessions.

What if he refuses?

Then coaching isn't the right step yet, and pushing harder usually backfires. Take care of yourself, set your own boundaries and keep the door open. Groups like Al-Anon and Nar-Anon support families of people who drink or use. My Omaha resources page lists more local options.

How do I help my husband who drinks too much?

Start by talking when he's sober and calm, not in the middle of a fight. Be specific about what you've seen and how it affects you and the kids. Skip the labels. Offer one next step, like a free call with a coach or a doctor visit. Get support for yourself too, whatever he decides.

My story

I grew up in North Omaha. I know what chaos feels like.

My mom struggled with meth. My dad wasn't around. I spent time in juvenile detention and carried that chaos into adulthood.

In 2011 I started changing how I lived. There was no single big moment. I kept showing up. I kept my word more often. I learned to sit with a feeling without letting it run the house.

Dad came home. Dad stayed.

I'm a father of four boys. Being present with them matters more to me than looking like I have it all figured out. That is the kind of man I help other men become.

Questions

Straight answers

What does a life coach do?

A life coach helps you get clear on what you want, build a simple plan and stick to it. With me that means weekly sessions, honest questions and accountability. We look at where your days go, what keeps knocking you off track and what to do on a bad day. You do the work. I help you keep showing up for it.

How much does a life coach cost in Omaha?

My coaching costs $149 to $399 a month. Starter is $149 for two 45-minute sessions, Core Coaching is $249 for four, and Focused Support is $399 for four 60-minute sessions. The first three Founding Clients get Core Coaching for $199 a month for three months. In-person sessions add $40 to cover the room. The first call is free. See full pricing.

Do I need a life coach or a therapist?

You need a therapist if you are dealing with a mental health condition, trauma that is taking over, or thoughts of harming yourself. A coach helps a stable man build structure, habits and follow-through. I am a non-clinical coach, not a therapist. Many men do both. If I think you need more than coaching, I will tell you and point you to licensed help.

What happens on the free discovery call?

The free call is 20 minutes on the phone. You tell me what keeps happening, what you have tried and what you want different. I ask a few straight questions and tell you honestly whether I can help. If it is a fit, we pick a plan and a start date. If not, I will point you somewhere better. No pressure either way.

Do you offer evening and Saturday sessions?

Yes. I coach Tuesday to Friday from 5:00 to 8:00 PM and Saturday from 11:00 AM to 1:00 PM, Central time. Sunday and Monday are closed. Evenings and Saturdays exist on purpose: most men I work with have jobs and kids, and they cannot leave work at 2 PM to talk about their life.

You know something needs to change. You just haven't changed it.

Most men don't call a coach when everything is on fire. They call when they're tired of the slow leak. The job that eats every evening. The short fuse at home. The drinking that's "not a problem" but shows up more than it should. The goals that have been on the list for five years.

You've probably tried to fix it alone. New planner. New gym membership. A big talk with yourself on Sunday night. Then Tuesday shows up, you're tired, and the old pattern wins again.

That's not a character flaw. It's what happens when nobody is checking in and the plan only works on good days. A plan matters most when you're angry, tired, broke, lonely, or ready to quit. That's the plan we build.

What we work on

Whatever is actually getting in your way

Every man is different, so coaching is too. These are the things that come up most.

Direction

Getting clear on what you want the next few years to look like, then breaking it down until it fits in a week.

Structure

Mornings, evenings, sleep and the basics. Most men feel better fast once the day has a shape again.

Follow-through

Small commitments you report back on. Keeping your word to yourself is where self-respect comes back.

Anger and stress

Stop before you react. Notice what sets you off and build a pause between the feeling and the words.

Home life

Being present with your partner and kids instead of just in the room. Better talks, fewer blowups.

Confidence

Less second-guessing. Making a decision, owning it and moving on, even when you're not sure.

How sessions work

Evenings, Saturdays, and wherever works for you

We start with a free 20-minute call. If it's a fit, the first session maps your week and picks the two or three changes that matter most. After that we meet weekly or every other week, depending on your plan.

  • In person at your location or a private meeting space in Omaha, by appointment. Some men prefer a walk-and-talk on the Keystone Trail or around Zorinsky Lake.
  • Video from home, the office or the truck.
  • Phone when that's all you have time for.

Hours: Tue–Fri 5:00–8:00 PM · Sat 11:00 AM–1:00 PM · Sun & Mon closed. I keep evenings and Saturdays open because most men can't leave work at 2 PM to talk about their life.

What changes

Small, boring wins that add up

I won't promise you a new life in 30 days. Nobody honest can. Here's what men usually notice when they keep showing up:

  • Evenings at home are calmer and shorter on blowups.
  • You keep more of the promises you make, starting with the small ones.
  • Mornings have a plan, so the day stops running you.
  • You make decisions faster and second-guess less.
  • Your partner and kids notice you're actually there.
  • Bad days still happen. They just don't wreck the whole week.

Honest fit

Who this is not for

  • Men who want someone to agree with them every week. I'll be respectful, and I'll be straight.
  • Men looking for a quick fix or a guaranteed result.
  • Anyone in crisis or needing mental health care, medical care or therapy. Call or text 988 for crisis help, and I can point you to licensed professionals.
  • Men who are only here because someone made them. Coaching only works if you choose it.

Skeptical? Good. Plenty of men come in not believing in any of this. That's fine. Give it a free 20 minutes and decide for yourself.

Questions

Life coaching for men: common questions

What is men's life coaching?

Men's life coaching is one-on-one coaching built around the pressures most men carry quietly: work, money, marriage, kids, anger and habits. We set a simple plan and meet every week so you keep it. It is practical and direct. You talk, I ask straight questions, and you leave with a few things to do before next time.

Do I have to be in crisis to work with a coach?

No. Most men I work with are functioning fine on paper. They go to work, pay bills and show up for their kids, but they feel stuck, tired or angry more than they want to. Coaching is for building something better, not for emergencies. If you are in crisis, call or text 988 right now.

What if I am not a talker?

That is fine. A lot of men are not. We keep it practical: what happened this week, what got in the way, what you will do next. Some men open up more on a walk-and-talk than sitting across a table, so we can do that too. You do not need the right words. Honest ones are enough.

How often do we meet?

Most men meet weekly. Core Coaching is four 45-minute sessions a month for $249. Starter is two sessions a month for $149, which suits men who need a steady check-in more than a big overhaul. Focused Support gives you four 60-minute sessions for $399. Sessions run evenings and Saturdays.

Is life coaching for men in Omaha only in person?

No. You can meet in person in Omaha, by video or by phone. In-person sessions happen at your location or a private meeting space by appointment and cost $40 extra to cover the room. Video and phone cost nothing extra and work well for men with long commutes or travel.

A plain list of places that help men and families in the Omaha metro. Coaching is one tool. These are others. Save this page or share it with someone who needs it.

Need immediate crisis help? Call or text 988. Need local services or resources? Call 211. Coaching is not crisis support. If you are in danger, call 911.

Right now: crisis and urgent help

If you or someone else is in danger, call 911. These lines are free, confidential and open 24/7.

  • 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (opens in a new tab)

    Call: 988

    Call or text 988, or chat online, any time. For anyone in emotional distress or worried about someone else.

  • Veterans Crisis Line (opens in a new tab)

    Call: 988, then press 1

    For veterans, service members and their families. Text 838255 also works.

  • Boys Town National Hotline (opens in a new tab)

    Call: 1-800-448-3000

    Based in Omaha. Free, 24/7 support for kids, teens and parents in any kind of trouble.

  • Nebraska Family Helpline (opens in a new tab)

    Call: 1-888-866-8660

    For Nebraska parents and families worried about a child or family member. Answered 24/7.

Local services and basic needs

Housing, food, utilities, jobs and legal help. 211 is the best first call when you are not sure where to start.

  • 211 Nebraska (opens in a new tab)

    Call: 211

    Free, confidential referrals to local help in Omaha and across Nebraska: rent, food, utilities, transport and more.

  • 211 Iowa (Council Bluffs) (opens in a new tab)

    Call: 211

    The same kind of local referral line for Council Bluffs and the rest of Iowa.

  • Heartland Family Service (opens in a new tab)

    Omaha and Council Bluffs nonprofit offering family support, housing, recovery and mental health programs.

  • Siena Francis House (opens in a new tab)

    Omaha shelter and recovery programs for people experiencing homelessness.

    Omaha shelter, meals and long-term recovery programs for men and families.

  • Legal Aid of Nebraska (opens in a new tab)

    Free civil legal help for low-income Nebraskans, including family and custody issues.

Is coaching worth it?

Look at what the old pattern already costs

$249 a month is real money. So is the cost of staying stuck. Think about the last year: the nights lost to drinking or the phone, the work you didn't go after, the arguments at home, the weekends you spent recovering instead of living.

Coaching is worth it if you use it. That means showing up, being honest and doing the small things between sessions. If you do, most men find it pays for itself in calmer evenings, better decisions and promises kept.

If you won't use it, it's not worth it, and I'll tell you that on the free call.

Price context

How these prices compare

Across the US, one-on-one life coaching commonly runs anywhere from about $75 to $300 or more for a single session, and monthly packages often land between $200 and $1,000. Coaches with big brands and executive clients can charge far more.

My plans work out to roughly $62 to $100 per session. I priced them so working men in Omaha can afford weekly support, not just executives with a company card. Every session is one-on-one with me.

Questions

Pricing questions

How much does a life coach cost in Omaha?

With me, coaching costs $149 to $399 a month depending on how often we meet and for how long. Starter is $149, Core Coaching is $249 and Focused Support is $399. The first three Founding Clients pay $199 a month for three months of Core Coaching. In-person sessions add $40 each. The first 20-minute call is free.

Why do you post your prices when most coaches don't?

Because you should know what something costs before you spend time on a sales call. Men I work with have bills and families. Clear prices let you decide if coaching fits your budget before we ever talk. If it doesn't fit right now, that's okay. The free resources on this site are still yours.

Is the in-person fee per session or per month?

Per session. Each in-person session adds $40 to cover the cost of a private room. If we meet at your location or do a walk-and-talk outdoors, ask about it on the free call. Video and phone sessions never have an extra fee, and they work the same way.

Can I switch plans later?

Yes. Plenty of men start on Core Coaching and move to Starter once habits are steady, or step up to Focused Support during a hard season. We look at it together every month or so. The goal is the least coaching that still keeps you moving, not the most I can sell you.

What is the Founding Client rate?

The first three clients get Core Coaching, four 45-minute sessions a month, for $199 a month instead of $249, with a three-month commitment ($597 total). It is my way of thanking the first men who trust me with their time. Once those three spots are filled, the rate closes.

Do you take insurance or HSA cards?

No. Coaching is not a medical service, so health insurance does not cover it and it is not usually HSA or FSA eligible. Some employers cover coaching through professional development budgets, so it can be worth asking yours.

  • Messages you send. When you use a form, we receive your name, phone, email (if given), your message, your contact preferences, the page you sent it from and any campaign tags in the link you clicked (UTM codes). Forms are processed by our host, Netlify.
  • Bookings. If you book a call, Calendly handles the booking under its own privacy policy.
  • Calls and texts. If you call or text, your number and message are stored on Roland's phone.

Third-party content

Videos from YouTube load only when you press play, using YouTube's privacy-enhanced mode. The Google Map loads only when you choose to show it. Each service has its own privacy policy.

How we use it

Only to reply to you, schedule calls and provide coaching. We do not sell, rent or trade your information. We do not add you to a mailing list without asking.

Coaching conversations

What you share in coaching stays private, except where someone is at risk of serious harm or the law requires disclosure. Coaching conversations are not legally privileged. Details are covered on your first call and in the coaching terms.

How long we keep it

Form messages are kept as long as needed to respond and for basic business records, then deleted. You can ask us to delete your information at any time.

Your choices

Email roland@rolandnielson.com to see, correct or delete what we have about you.

Children

This site and coaching are for adults. We do not knowingly collect information from anyone under 18.

Rebuilding after addiction · Omaha

Life after the hardest chapter

Coaching from someone who has lived addiction, chaos and jail cells, and rebuilt anyway. For men building structure, routine and trust after a hard stretch.

Book a Free Discovery Call Call or Text Roland

Last updated October 16, 2026

Need immediate crisis help? Call or text 988. Need local services or resources? Call 211. Coaching is not crisis support. If you are in danger, call 911.

Why I do this

People get quiet when you talk about recovery. I don't.

I grew up in North Omaha with a mom who struggled with meth and a dad who wasn't around. I spent time in juvenile detention and carried that chaos into adulthood. I lived addiction. I've sat in jail cells and at funerals.

In 2011 I started changing how I lived. No single big moment. I kept showing up, kept my word more often, and learned to sit with a feeling without letting it run the house.

I'm not hiding my story to make anybody comfortable. Addiction doesn't look one way. It looks like real people who decided they wanted better. If that's you, I want to help you build what comes next.

What we work on

Building a life worth staying sober for

Getting clean is a beginning. What you build around it is what keeps it.

Daily structure

Wake time, meals, work, meetings, sleep. Empty hours are dangerous hours, so we fill them on purpose.

A plan for the hard hours

A plan matters most when you're angry, tired, broke, lonely, or ready to quit. We write it down before you need it.

Accountability

Weekly sessions where you report what you said you'd do. Honest, not harsh.

Rebuilding trust

With your kids, partner, parents and employer. Kept promises, small and often.

Work and money

Getting back to steady work, handling debt and building a little stability you can stand on.

Who you are now

Shame keeps men stuck. We work on owning the past without living in it.

How sessions work

Alongside your support, not instead of it

If you have meetings, a sponsor, professional care or an aftercare plan, keep them. Coaching works next to them and focuses on the rest of your week: routines, relationships, work and the goals you've been putting off.

  • Free 20-minute call first. Be honest about where you are.
  • Weekly sessions in person in Omaha, by video or by phone.
  • Evenings and Saturdays: Tue–Fri 5:00–8:00 PM · Sat 11:00 AM–1:00 PM · Sun & Mon closed.
  • Men who want a longer, deeper reset often choose the Rebuild Program.

Want local meetings and groups too? See my list of Omaha resources for men.

What changes

Your story is real. So is your comeback.

No promises about outcomes. Recovery is yours. Here's what men rebuilding often notice when they stay with it:

  • Days have a shape, so cravings and boredom have less room.
  • You have a written plan for the worst hours of the week.
  • Family starts to believe you again, slowly, because you're consistent.
  • You stop hiding your story and start using it.
  • Goals you'd given up on get back on the calendar.

Plain and clear

What this is not

I'm a non-clinical life coach. I am not a counselor, therapist, doctor or certified peer-recovery specialist. Coaching is not addiction treatment, detox, medication management or crisis care, and it is not a substitute for any of them.

If you need any of that, I'll help you find it, and coaching can continue alongside it. If you are in danger right now, call 911. For crisis support, call or text 988. For local services, call 211.

Questions

Questions about coaching in recovery

Is a sober coach or recovery coach the same as what you do?

Not exactly. I am a life coach who has lived through addiction and rebuilt, not a certified recovery professional. I help men build structure, routine and accountability for the life they are rebuilding. I do not run a program, provide sober monitoring or replace meetings, a sponsor or professional care. Coaching sits alongside those.

Do I have to be sober to work with you?

You need to be stable enough to make and keep small commitments. If you are actively using and want to stop, the first step is getting the right support, and I can help you find it. If you are early in recovery or a few years in, coaching can help you build the rest of your life around it.

Will you tell me which recovery path to follow?

No. I don't believe one program, meeting or method works for everybody. Some men do AA or NA, some do SMART Recovery, some lean on faith, family or a professional. We look at your life and use what helps. If something is working for you, we protect it.

Can coaching help me rebuild trust with my family?

Yes. Trust comes back slowly, through kept promises, not big speeches. We work on what you can control: showing up on time, being honest about small things, calling when you said you would, and owning past damage without making it about you. Your family decides when to trust again. Your job is to be consistent.

What about life after rehab in Omaha?

Coming home after rehab is often harder than being there. The structure is gone, old people and places are close, and everyone is watching. Coaching helps you rebuild a daily routine, plan for the hardest hours of the week and stay accountable. It works best alongside your aftercare plan, meetings and support network.

Is it confidential?

Yes. What you share stays between us unless someone is at risk of serious harm or the law requires it. I won't talk to your family, employer or probation officer without your written permission. Coaching is not legally privileged the way some professions are, and I explain that on the free call.

The Rebuild Program

A 3–6 month, high-accountability program for men who are done patching things and ready to rebuild: habits, mindset, relationships, discipline and long-term goals.

Book a call to apply Call (402) 577-0738

Last updated October 16, 2026

Who it's for

For men who know a weekly chat won't be enough

Some men need a steady check-in. Others need a full rebuild. If you're coming out of addiction, a divorce, a lost job or years of drifting, and you're ready to put real effort in for a few months, this is built for you.

  • You've tried to change on your own and keep ending up back at the start.
  • More than one area of life needs work at the same time.
  • You want someone in your corner between sessions, not just during them.
  • You're willing to commit for 3 or 6 months.

Not sure if you need the full program? Start with accountability coaching or compare all coaching plans.

Three phases

Stabilize. Rebuild. Sustain.

Every man's timeline is different. This is the shape most programs follow.

01

Stabilize

First month

Stop the bleeding. Sleep, routine, money basics and a written plan for the hardest hours of your week. We find what keeps knocking you down and put guardrails around it.

02

Rebuild

Middle months

Habits, discipline and relationships. Keeping your word to yourself and others. Hard conversations at home. Work and goals you have been putting off. Weekly sessions plus check-ins between them.

03

Sustain

Final stretch

Make it yours. We test the plan against real life, prepare for setbacks, and set long-term goals so the changes hold after the program ends.

A typical week

What a week in the program looks like

Session day. We start with the same question every time: did you do what you said? Then we look at what got in the way, adjust the plan and set the next few commitments. Evenings or Saturday, in person, by video or by phone.

Midweek check-in. A short check between sessions, usually around the point in the week where men tend to slip. It's not a lecture. It's a reminder that someone is paying attention, and a chance to fix a bad Tuesday before it becomes a bad month.

The weekend. For a lot of men this is the hardest stretch: unstructured time, family pressure, old habits. Your plan covers it on purpose.

Why 3 to 6 months? Because most of what we're changing took years to build. A few weeks is enough to feel better. A few months is enough to become someone who keeps it going without me.

What's included

More contact. More accountability.

  • Weekly one-on-one sessions in person in Omaha, by video or by phone.
  • Between-session check-ins so a bad Tuesday doesn't turn into a bad month.
  • A full rebuild plan covering habits, mindset, relationships, discipline and long-term goals.
  • A written plan for your hardest hours, for when you're angry, tired, broke, lonely, or ready to quit.
  • Regular reviews to look at what's working and change what isn't.
  • Evening and Saturday times that fit around work and family.

Commitment

3 months or 6 months

3 months suits men with one or two big areas to rebuild and a decent foundation to stand on.

6 months suits men rebuilding after addiction or a major life change, or anyone who wants time for the new habits to really set.

Pricing is shared on the free call. Spots are limited so I can actually be there between sessions.

Questions

About the Rebuild Program

How is the Rebuild Program different from regular coaching?

The Rebuild Program is longer, deeper and more hands-on. Regular plans give you scheduled sessions. The Rebuild Program adds check-ins between sessions, a full plan across habits, mindset, relationships, discipline and long-term goals, and a 3- or 6-month commitment so we have time to do real work instead of patching things week to week.

How much does the Rebuild Program cost?

Pricing is shared on the free call, because the program is shaped around each man and his commitment length. It costs more than the standard plans because it includes more contact between sessions. You will know the full price before you commit to anything.

Why do I have to apply?

Because it only works for men who are ready to commit. I keep a small number of Rebuild spots so I can actually be available between sessions. The application is just the free call: we talk, I ask honest questions, and we both decide whether this is the right fit right now.

What if I need to stop partway through?

Life happens. We talk about the exact terms before you start, including what happens if something serious comes up. My goal is not to trap anybody in a contract. It is to give you a long enough runway that the changes stick.

Is the Rebuild Program only for men in recovery?

No. It is for any man who wants a full reset: after addiction, divorce, a job loss, a health scare, or just years of drifting. Some of the men who choose it are rebuilding after addiction, and the program works well alongside meetings or professional support.

The Rebuild Program is non-clinical coaching. It is not addiction treatment or therapy and does not replace them.
